title: Get Ahead at Work · Episode 1
chapters: Giving and receiving feedback at work

units.t: Get Ahead at Work. Episode one.
In this episode: Time management that works, Writing work emails people read, Giving and receiving feedback at work and Running a meeting worth attending.
Part one. Time management that works.
You can't make more time.
But you can stop losing it to the wrong things.
Urgent versus important.
In a 1954 speech, US President Dwight Eisenhower quoted a former college president: 'I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important.
The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent.'
The Eisenhower matrix sorts tasks into four boxes.
Urgent and important: do it now, such as a crisis or deadline.
Important but not urgent: schedule it, such as exercise, planning, relationships and learning.
Urgent but not important: delegate or minimise, such as most interruptions and many emails.
Neither: drop it.
Most people live in the urgent boxes.
The biggest gains come from protecting time for the important-but-not-urgent work.
How time misleads us.
In 1955, historian C.
Northcote Parkinson wrote that 'work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion.'
Give yourself a week for a report and it takes a week.
Timeboxing, setting a fixed block for a task, uses this to your advantage.
Decide what 'good enough' looks like first, so perfectionism doesn't swallow the extra time.
Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky named the planning fallacy: we underestimate how long tasks take, even when similar ones ran long before.
We imagine the best case and forget interruptions.
The Sydney Opera House was due to open in early 1963 and opened in 1973, ten years late and hugely over budget.
Check how long similar tasks really took, then add a buffer, often 50% or more.
Block time, protect focus.
A to-do list tells you what to do, not when.
Time blocking means scheduling tasks in your calendar as if they were meetings: 9 to 10.
30 am, write proposal.
It shows how much time you really have and reduces decision fatigue.
Put demanding work in your peak energy hours, often the morning, and leave buffer blocks for the unexpected.
Multitasking is mostly a myth.
The brain switches between demanding tasks rather than doing both at once, and each switch costs time and attention.
Research on interruptions suggests it can take many minutes to refocus on a complex task.
Batch small tasks like emails into set times and turn off non-essential alerts.
An hour of uninterrupted work can beat a distracted afternoon.
The two-minute rule.
David Allen, author of Getting Things Done, suggests a simple rule: if a task takes less than two minutes, do it immediately instead of writing it down or putting it off.
Reply to the quick email, file the document, book the appointment.
It stops small tasks piling up into a mental burden.
Allen's broader insight is that your mind is for having ideas, not holding them.
Capture every other task in one trusted list or app so your brain can stop trying to remember everything.
Review and say no.
Once a week, often Friday afternoon or Sunday evening, spend 20 to 30 minutes reviewing.
Look at what you finished, what's still open and what's coming up.
Clear your inboxes and notes into your task list.
Choose your three most important priorities for the week ahead and block time for them.
It stops tasks slipping through the cracks and turns vague stress into a plan.
Then protect those priorities.
Every yes is a no to something else, so ask what a new commitment will replace.
You can decline politely: 'Thanks for thinking of me, but I can't take that on right now.'
Some people use a rule: if it's not a clear yes, it's a no.
The key idea: The Eisenhower matrix sorts tasks by urgency and importance, and the biggest gains come from protecting important-but-not-urgent work.
Part two. Writing work emails people read.
Most work emails get skimmed in seconds.
A few simple habits make yours the ones that get read, understood and acted on.
Write for a skimmer.
Your reader is probably on a phone between meetings, deciding from the subject line and first couple of lines whether to act now, deal with it later or ignore it.
Before writing, ask: what do I want this person to know, and what do I want them to do?
If you can't answer both in a sentence, you're not ready to write.
Treat the subject line as a headline.
'Quick question' or 'Update' says nothing and is hard to find later.
Try 'Approval needed: Q3 marketing budget by Friday'.
Prefixes like 'Action:' or 'FYI:' help people triage.
If the topic changes, change the subject line.
A very short message can go entirely in the subject, followed by 'EOM', end of message.
Bottom line up front.
Many of us were taught to write chronologically: background, then reasoning, then the point.
At work, flip it.
Put the bottom line up front, a habit known as BLUF, borrowed from military writing.
Start with the conclusion, decision or request, then add context for anyone who wants it.
Compare 'Following our discussion last week, and after reviewing the supplier quotes, I've looked at our options...'
with 'I recommend we go with Supplier B; it's $4,000 cheaper and can deliver two weeks sooner.
Details below.'
The second version can be understood and acted on even if the reader stops after one sentence.
Brief, clear requests.
Aim for an email that fits on a phone screen.
Cut warm-up phrases like 'I just wanted to reach out to touch base regarding'.
Stick to one topic per email, or one of them gets forgotten, and use short paragraphs.
Number multiple questions so the reader can reply 'Yes to 1, no to 2'.
If it needs pages of explanation, attach a document or book a meeting.
Vague requests get vague results.
'Thoughts?'
invites delay; 'Can you confirm by Thursday 5 pm whether the venue booking for 40 people is okay?'
gets an answer.
Name the person when writing to several, because a request addressed to everyone is often done by no one.
Offer options, 'Does 10 am or 2 pm suit?'
, and say 'No reply needed' when it applies.
Tone and channel.
Without voice and facial expression, readers tend to read neutral messages as more negative than intended.
A clipped 'Fine.'
or 'Per my last email' can land as irritation.
In Australian workplaces, 'Hi Sam' and 'Thanks' or 'Kind regards' are standard.
Avoid sarcasm, excessive exclamation marks and ALL CAPS, and match your reader's formality.
Email is poor for some jobs.
If it's urgent, call.
If it's emotional, such as feedback, conflict or bad news, talk in person or by video.
If a chain goes back and forth three or four times, have a quick conversation, then send a short summary of what was agreed.
Never send an email while angry: save it as a draft and reread it later.
Work emails can be forwarded and may be used in legal disputes.
Before you hit send.
A thirty-second check prevents most email embarrassments.
Are the right people in To, who must act, and Cc, who just need to know?
Use Reply All only when everyone genuinely needs your reply.
Did you attach the file you mentioned?
Is your key point in the first lines, with any request and deadline clear?
Are names spelt correctly?
Read anything sensitive aloud and imagine how it sounds to someone having a bad day.
Many email programs let you delay or schedule sending.
That gives you a window to catch mistakes and avoids late-night emails that pressure colleagues to reply outside hours.
Then send, and move on.
The key idea: Assume your reader is busy and skimming, so make the subject line and opening say what the email is and what you need.
Part three. Giving and receiving feedback at work.
Feedback can lift a team or wreck a week.
A few practical techniques make it clearer, kinder and far more useful.
Why feedback goes wrong.
Think of the last time someone said 'Can I give you some feedback?'
Your heart probably sped up.
Feedback feels personal because work is tied to our sense of competence and belonging.
Delivered badly, it makes people stop listening and start defending.
The common problems are easy to spot.
Vague feedback, such as 'be more professional', gives nothing to act on.
Feedback saved for an annual review arrives months too late.
Feedback mixed with frustration sounds like an attack.
And generic praise like 'great job' feels hollow.
The good news is that giving and receiving feedback are both skills, and a few simple structures make conversations shorter, clearer and less painful.
Situation, behaviour, impact.
One widely used structure, developed by the Center for Creative Leadership, has three steps.
Name the situation: 'In Tuesday's client meeting'.
Describe the specific behaviour you saw or heard, without guessing at motives: 'you interrupted the client twice'.
Explain the impact: 'they seemed frustrated and we did not get the full picture'.
This keeps the conversation on facts rather than character judgements like 'you are rude'.
Then pause and ask, 'How did it look from your side?'
There may be context you missed.
The same structure works for praise: 'When you stayed calm with that upset customer this morning, the whole queue relaxed, and she thanked us on the way out.'
Timing and the future.
Feedback is most useful within a day or two, but not in the heat of the moment.
If you are angry, wait.
Give criticism in private, never in front of colleagues or customers.
Ask first: 'Have you got ten minutes?'
Avoid important feedback by text or chat, where tone is easily misread.
Once you have heard their view, shift forward.
Ask 'What could we try next time?'
People commit more to solutions they helped shape.
Make any request clear, such as 'please let clients finish before you jump in', and agree on one or two changes, not ten.
Then follow up and notice improvement.
Think of feedback as coaching: the goal is not to win an argument about the past but to make next week better.
Receiving feedback well.
When feedback lands, your instinct may be to explain, justify or counterattack.
Try to resist, at least at first.
Breathe, listen to the whole message and ask clarifying questions: 'Can you give me an example?'
or 'What would good look like?'
Summarise what you heard to check you understood.
Then thank them, even if you disagree, because giving feedback takes effort and some courage.
You do not have to accept every point on the spot.
It is fine to say, 'I want to think about that and come back to you.'
Later, sort what you heard into three piles: useful and true, partly true and simply not right.
Act on the first pile.
Asking and leading.
Waiting for feedback means getting it on someone else's schedule, often when something has gone wrong.
Ask instead, and be specific, because 'Any feedback?'
usually produces 'No, all good'.
Try 'What is one thing I could do to make my reports more useful?'
Ask a mix of people, including those who report to you, who may need reassurance that honesty is safe.
Leaders shape feedback culture more than any policy.
If you get defensive, people stay quiet and you lose early warnings.
If you thank people for raising concerns, they learn it is safe.
Hold regular one to ones, and keep a light record so reviews hold no surprises.
Keep feedback separate from formal performance or disciplinary processes, which have their own rules.
The Fair Work Ombudsman publishes free guides for managers and employees.
The key idea: Most feedback fails because it is vague, late or delivered in a way that triggers defence.
Part four. Running a meeting worth attending.
Most of us have sat through a meeting that should have been an email.
Here is how to run one people are glad they came to.
The cost of a meeting.
Picture eight people in a one hour meeting.
That is not one hour of work.
It is eight hours, nearly a full working day.
If the meeting drifts, ends without a decision and needs a follow up, the cost doubles.
Bad meetings also drain energy, interrupt focused work and teach people that their time does not matter.
Good ones can settle in thirty minutes a question that would take two weeks of emails, and get everyone moving in the same direction.
The difference is rarely luck.
Good meetings are designed, and anyone can learn how, whether you lead a team or are organising your first catch up.
Meeting or not, and who.
If you only need to share information, an email, short document or recorded update is often better.
Meetings suit things that need live conversation: decisions, tricky problems, building agreement, brainstorming and sensitive issues.
Finish this line: 'By the end of this meeting, we will have...'
If you cannot, you are not ready to book.
Put that sentence at the top of the invitation.
Invite only people who must decide, hold information you cannot get elsewhere or must carry out the outcome.
Others can read a summary.
But leaving out a key person often means redoing the meeting.
Respect different working hours, and consider twenty five or fifty minutes instead of an hour, leaving a buffer between calls.
Write a real agenda.
An agenda that says 'budget, rosters, other business' tells nobody what to prepare.
Turn each item into a question with a time: 'Which of the two venue quotes do we accept?
Ten minutes.
Read the attached comparison first.'
Put the most important item first, while energy is high, and send the agenda and any reading at least a day ahead.
Ask people to come prepared, and say so plainly.
Some teams start with a few quiet minutes to read the key document together, which levels the playing field and means nobody bluffs.
If someone wants to add an item, ask them to tell you beforehand.
An agenda is a promise about how you will use people's time.
Run the room.
Begin on time, even if someone is late, and restate the purpose in a sentence.
As chair, your job is to guide, not dominate.
Watch the clock and gently steer drifting conversations: 'Good point, let us park it.'
Keep a visible parking lot list so people know side issues have not been ignored.
Draw out quieter people by asking them directly, and politely rein in those who speak at length.
In hybrid meetings, make sure remote attendees can hear, see shared material and get a fair turn, perhaps by calling on them first.
If the discussion is going in circles, summarise where things stand and ask what is needed to decide.
End and follow up.
The last five minutes matter most, so protect them.
Read back what was decided in plain words.
List the actions: what, who and by when.
An action without a name next to it usually does not happen.
Check nobody disagrees, then finish a few minutes early.
A good test: could every attendee tell a colleague, in a sentence or two, what was decided and what they must do next?
Within a few hours, send a brief note covering decisions, actions with owners and dates, and open questions.
Store it where the team can find it.
Check on actions when due.
Review regular meetings now and then, and be willing to shorten or cancel them.
The key idea: A meeting uses everyone's time at once, so its cost is multiplied by the number of people in the room.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. In the Eisenhower matrix, what should you do with important but not urgent tasks?
Answer. Schedule them.
Question two. Which subject line is most effective?
Answer. Approval needed: Q3 budget by Friday.
Question three. Which of these is the most useful kind of feedback?
Answer. Specific and timely, so the person knows what to change.
Question four. Why is a one hour meeting with eight people costly?
Answer. It adds up to about eight hours of work time.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
